title: Light poured out
hook: sunlight seems poured down but is never used up (Meditations 8.57)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the pure spring. Your line was the spring runs clear. When something clouded you, did the water clear? Day six hundred four.

Sit in a room with one window on a sunny afternoon and watch the patch of light on the floor. It's been pouring in all day. More light every minute, and the window never runs dry. The sun never sends a bill. Nobody has to refill it. Marcus noticed the same plain thing, sunlight coming in, and found in it a picture of how a mind should move through the world. Today: light poured out.
screen: `A PATCH OF LIGHT ON THE FLOOR.` → `POURING IN ALL DAY.` → `LIGHT POURED OUT.`

segments.voice: First, the puzzle. The sun's light seems poured down, Marcus says, spread out in every direction, and yet it isn't poured away. It isn't used up. The spreading, he says, is a kind of stretching out. Second, his word game. The Greek word for rays is aktines, and Marcus says they're called that from a verb meaning to be stretched out. It's his own word play, and the point isn't the dictionary. It's the picture: light reaches out without leaving its source. Third, the beam in a dark room. Watch, he says, sunlight coming through a narrow opening into a dark house. It travels in a straight line, and when it meets something solid that blocks it, it rests there. It doesn't slide off. It doesn't fall. It just lights up what's in front of it. Fourth, the mind. That's how Marcus wants his own mind to pour itself out: not emptied, not crashing violently into whatever stands in the way, but resting on it, and lighting whatever will take the light. And if something refuses it, he says, that thing only deprives itself. So attention, warmth, effort: given like sunlight, they can reach far and still not run out, as long as they're poured, not thrown.
screen: `POURED DOWN, NEVER USED UP.` · `AKTINES: MARCUS'S WORD PLAY.` · `THE BEAM RESTS ON WHAT IT MEETS.` · `A MIND THAT POURS, NOT CRASHES.` · then, large: `POURED OUT.`

segments.voice: If you can, move into sunlight: a window, a doorway, a patch on the floor. If it's night, picture one. Let the light rest on your hands. Notice that it doesn't push. It doesn't rush. It just arrives and stays. Breathe. Now think of one person you'll see today, and imagine your attention reaching them like that: steady, warm, not forcing, not running out. The bell holds the time.
Light poured out. Marcus's picture of sunlight: spread in every direction, never used up, resting on what it meets. So a mind should reach out. Today's word.
Your line: poured out. Give your attention to one person today the way light comes through a window: steady, not forced. Notice whether it runs out. Day six hundred four.

howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus use sunlight as a daily reminder: a few minutes in the light, and then attention given to others the way it falls, steady and unforced.

fork.setup: you're the beam of light coming into a dark room, and you hit a wall. what do you do?
options: crash against it until it gives.
slide off and go somewhere else.
rest on it, and light up what's there.
fork.reveal: Marcus says the light stays fixed where it meets a solid body, neither glancing off nor falling, and lights what receives it.

original.note: Greek: a ray of light (plural aktines). Marcus links it, playfully, to a verb meaning to stretch out.

trapdoor: what you thought: sunshine is nice.
what it means: the mind can reach out like light, resting on what it meets, without being used up or crashing into obstacles.
what a scholar hears: Marcus ties aktis, a ray, to ekteinesthai, to be stretched out, and makes the word play carry his point: light is extension, not loss.

notes: 8.57 paraphrased: the sun appears poured down and diffused but not effused; diffusion is extension; aktines named from ekteinesthai; light through a narrow opening into a dark room goes straight and rests on a solid body; so should the mind's outpouring be, not violent, illuminating what receives it; what does not admit it deprives itself. Confirm.
Confirm that the aktis/ekteinesthai derivation is not accepted by standard lexicons (it is generally treated as Marcus's own etymology).
